sources.title: Aquarium fish are more aggressive in reduced environments, new study finds
Cách Xử Lý Cá Cảnh Bị Thương Khi Bị Tấn Công
Cá Bị Nấm Xâm Nhập Vết Cắn Tranh Giành Lãnh Thổ: Cách Xử Lý Tổn Thương Sâu Chống Thối Thịt - Sài Gòn Cá Cảnh

facts.fact: Most aggression in an aquarium is over territory: fish defend places they use to rest, hide or breed.
Fish are most aggressive toward rivals of their own species and sex, because a territory often guards a breeding site, eggs or fry.
Fish set up a pecking order, and it can change as individual fish grow and mature.
As fish mature their territories grow, which keepers should plan for.
Colour, pattern and shape affect which fish get attacked; bettas (Betta splendens) may attack non-betta fish that are red, such as platies and serpae tetras.
Bullying weakens the victim's immune system, letting opportunistic pathogens such as chilodonella, costia, epistylis and bacteria cause serious disease.
Aggressive fish ram less dominant fish, stripping scales and tattering fins and inviting secondary bacterial infection; victims often die.
Aggression is common in cichlid tanks, especially Lake Malawi cichlids, and some Central American cichlids are nearly as bad.
Individual fish vary widely: the author has seen normally aggressive species behave mildly and normally mellow species kill tankmates in heavily stocked tanks.
Male betta (cá Betta) may attack any fish that comes near their spawning site.
Oscar is aggressive and may treat smaller fish as threats or prey.
Signs of fighting include split fins (different from the ragged edges of tail rot), fish suddenly hiding, fish changing territories, scrapes, torn lips, missing scales and missing eyes.
Fights often happen when nobody is watching, so the damage may only be noticed later.
Injured, bullied fish may hide, become lethargic, refuse food, swim slowly or avoid light.

Bite wounds from territorial fights can show a thick white fungal mass (Saprolegnia) on the flank, with swelling and redness around the wound, and the fish hides in corners or behind driftwood with clamped fins.
Overcrowding causes stress and poor water quality and drives aggression; the article suggests about 1 fish per 10–20 liters, depending on species.
Mixing incompatible species (aggressive with timid fish, predators with omnivores) and the breeding season, when males guard nests and young, drive attacks.
Fungal spores settle into open bite wounds within hours, especially in water with organic debris, and a fish that keeps being chased cannot heal.

In a study of juvenile Midas cichlids (Amphilophus citrinellus), fish in small tanks of the sizes pet owners use were more aggressive; aggression fell only in environments that were sufficiently large and complex.
In the Midas cichlid study, small changes to group size or habitat size alone had no clear effect on aggression.
Allow minor sparring first, because fish often settle the pecking order themselves.
If fighting persists, rearrange the decorations to force new territories, and add hiding places and visual barriers.
If separation is needed, put the bully, not the victim, in a net breeder for about a week, so it stays in view of the others but cannot attack.
Move seriously injured fish to a quarantine tank, for example a bare 5- or 10-gallon tank with a cover and a sponge filter.
For minor fight injuries: clean water, good food and isolation; options include a slime-coat conditioner and about a teaspoon of salt per gallon.
For severe infections after fights, antibiotics such as kanamycin, triple sulfa and furanoids (nifurpirinol, furazone) are mentioned.
Treat sick bullied fish in a dark, quiet hospital tank with an ich medication (copper or formalin/malachite green) plus a broad-spectrum antibiotic (Maracyn 2) given only in the food.
Before medicating a bitten fish, test that NH3 = 0.00 mg/L and NO2⁻ = 0.00 mg/L, aerate strongly 24/24 to keep DO ≥ 6.0 mg/L, and keep temperature changes within 0.5°C per hour.
Non-iodized salt at 1–3 g/L may be used, only for freshwater species that tolerate salt.
Isolate the injured fish and dab the wound with Povidone Iodine 5% on a cotton swab; after 4–5 days in clean water the wound should dry and new scales form.
Recovery takes about 1–2 weeks for minor fin tears, 2–4 weeks for scrapes or peeling skin, and 4–8+ weeks for serious injuries; avoid strong medicine unless symptoms are severe.
Redecorate when adding new fish so that newcomers do not start without a territory.
Non-territorial schooling fish such as tiger barbs are less likely to nip fins when kept in groups of at least six.
Match fish of similar aggression levels.

Stock mbuna and mixed Malawi tanks heavily: at least one 4" fish per two gallons, a minimum of 29 gallons and 15 fish, with heavy water changes and over-filtration; keep predator hap tanks lightly stocked.
Add new cichlids at least three at a time, keep lights off except for feeding or viewing, and keep the water cooler; the author keeps Malawi cichlids at 70 to 75°F.
Keep only males of peacocks and haps; mix sexes of mbuna only in heavily stocked tanks.
Adding rocks, plants and other obstacles and hiding places made Midas cichlids spend less time on aggressive displays and attacks.
Use plants, rocks or driftwood to create separate territories, and quarantine new fish for several days before adding them to the main tank.
A transparent acrylic divider can mark territories and stop chases; dimming the lights and adding rocks and driftwood as hiding spots reduce stress.
Repeatedly netting fish apart rarely solves fighting in the long term.
Removing the victim when its injuries are minor rewards the bully.
Keeping very aggressive cichlids such as some Melanochromis, Nimbochromis and predator haps without experience; juveniles are mellow but fully grown adults are often killers.
Giving Malawi cichlids caves lets them set up territories; adding fish one at a time and keeping two males of the same or similar hap or peacock species together are also mistakes.
Keeping long-finned guppies with Oscar can injure the guppies within days.
Leaving an injured fish with the aggressive group, or in water with organic sediment, lets bite wounds worsen.

The author of Aquarium Science warns that all these anti-aggression rules are only gross generalizations that work some of the time; the only reliable fix he found was moving one aggressor to another tank.
